title: Solo devs using AI coding agents: what do you still do by hand?
author: SpaceTime5920
selftext:
I've been making a small game mostly with an AI coding agent (Claude Code) doing the typing. It's been great for code, tests and boring tooling, like scripts that take screenshots and record short clips of the game. But some things I still want to do myself: deciding how the levels play, and testing on a real phone.

Curious how others split it:

1. What do you let the AI do completely?
2. What do you always do by hand, and why?
3. Any tool or workflow that surprised you, good or bad?

comments.author: Such--Balance
comments.body:
I extract all parameters to jsons and tweak them post-implementation of any new system.

Balance and feel are better left in your own hands i feel like.

replies.author: SpaceTime5920
replies.body: Same here, the feel is the part I won't hand over. Which numbers do you end up tweaking the most, things like speed and timing, or damage and costs?

comments.author: Heath_co
comments.body:
I don't tell the AI exactly how things should be coded, because it would likely find a better and more efficient way than I can with testing.

I provide the AI its best practices when coding. I wrote the principles that all new code should be reviewed against. I describe how the code should work on an abstract level, what the different components of systems are, and how they should interact with each other.

If I just tell an AI to code a new feature, it will be undisciplined and create duplicate code for everything. My job is to make sure the AI knows what is already in the codebase and what it should use to build new things.

replies.author: SpaceTime5920
replies.body: This matches my experience. I keep a file of rules the agent reads every session, like which checks to run and what not to touch, and it made a huge difference. Without it, it happily writes a second version of something that already exists.

comments.author: TheHabeo
comments.body:
Human testing, balance sheet,  lore and content  mechanic.

My game has 6 class, each with 2 ascendancies so 12 classes in total. Giving the AI sandbox testing for datapoint, then do human balancing with the dev tool at various point (early game, mid game, late, end) .

Play through the game on all the classes from the start to get an idea of early struggles, what's OP, whats underpowered, what bugs out or any utility feature that could make it more comfortable to play.

replies.author: NormieInTheMaking
replies.body: I have agents do the playtesting for balance issues. They can run thousands of runs easily and report the findings.

comments.author: axolotlgarden
comments.body: Testing, I found it can code well and critic well but is your game any good. That comes with human oversight

comments.author: kokutouchichi
comments.body:
Animation, level design, prop design and story/dialogue. I make the AI do the boring stuff the setup of colliders, assets and then I go in and make sure it's perfect. Or I'll do it first and set it up how I want and tell Claude or codex to copy what I've done. 

An example would be setting up a door in a doorway and making sure all the walls are flush around it. Then I point Claude to my example and have it mirror that all around the map.

There are so many examples in this sub of people trying to skip every single step in the process of gamedev and automate everything away and it shows.

replies.author: SpaceTime5920
replies.body: That's a smart way to do it: build one by hand exactly how you want it, then point the AI at it as the example. Your taste stays in it and it saves the boring repeat work. And agreed on the last part, you can usually tell when nobody actually played the thing.

replies.author: SQStudio
replies.body: That's what I do as well, it's draining to check all art is assembled properly for my game but there's no way I can let Claude do it on its own and even check it, there are things that it simply doesn't see and it has to be done manually

comments.author: VisibleBoard8186
comments.body: I check if my laptop is warm. If it is warm I don't turn on the screen, if it is cool I check if it is completed.

replies.author: SpaceTime5920
replies.body: HaHa 😄, The fan noise is my progress bar.

comments.author: Active_Specialist792
comments.body: I tell it what to do. AI does everything else.

comments.author: cristocanaro
comments.body: I do create, storyboard, lore, characters, art style direction, gameplay and game design sketches by hand, then I do the play testing by my hand after making the Ai run hundreads of iteration on every single game aspect related to mechanics and bug finding.

comments.author: shoukachidev
comments.body: music. Been making music for years and having games like deltarune prove what music can transport, i want that for my games aswell

comments.author: Any-Preparation7396
comments.body:
_"
Solo devs [...] what do you still do by hand?"_

If I'll tell you, I would probably get banned on Reddit.

/s

comments.author: s22stumarket
comments.body: I film the animations on myself but then I let AI to cut the video, process it through mocap software, clean the animation and put it to the game via fixed workflow (fixed in theory, because AI still disvovers ways to ignore some steps or create new ones).

comments.author: LifeStartsToday
comments.body:
1. code, event text, and translations into 5 languages. honestly almost all the typing  
2. every gameplay decision and balance call, and testing the actual build myself in unity. ai is confident even when the numbers feel wrong in play, so i only trust what i've played  
3. good surprise: shipped an ios game with no mac at all, just windows + unity cloud build. bad one: ai will "finish" a ui screen that looks nothing like the mockup unless you compare them side by side
